text: Every quantum circuit you build eventually ends in a measurement, and a measurement's outcome is random, governed by a probability distribution derived from the state's amplitudes. This lesson covers the probability concepts that let you reason precisely about what a quantum computer actually tells you, on average, across many runs.

A discrete probability distribution assigns a non-negative probability to each possible outcome, with all probabilities summing to 1. A qubit measured in the computational basis has exactly two outcomes, 0 and 1, with probabilities equal to the squared magnitudes of alpha and beta — the simplest possible distribution, and the same normalization condition you already know, just read as probabilities.

The expectation value is the sum of each outcome's value weighted by its probability — the formal meaning of 'average.' For a qubit measured in the Z basis, outcome 0 conventionally gets the value plus one and outcome 1 gets negative one. With P of 0 equal to 0.64 and P of 1 equal to 0.36, the expectation value works out to 0.64 times 1 plus 0.36 times negative 1, which is 0.28 — not one of the two individual outcomes, but their probability-weighted average.

Many real quantum algorithms, like the variational methods you'll study later, don't want a single measurement outcome — they want the expectation value of an operator, built by running the circuit many times and averaging. A single measurement is just one noisy sample; the expectation value only converges as the number of shots grows large, which is exactly why real quantum tools default to running a circuit hundreds or thousands of times rather than once.
Next lesson asks the natural follow-up question: how spread out are the actual outcomes around that average? Variance and standard deviation quantify that spread.
